
Bucket sort on the example of CLRS §8.4. Scatter, sort each bucket, gather. The buckets stay tiny because the keys are spread over the whole interval.

:::

### The expected-time argument {#sec-lts-a4-proof}

Let $n_i$ be the number of keys that land in bucket $i$. Scattering and gathering cost $\Theta(n)$; insertion sort on bucket $i$ costs $O(n_i^2)$. So the running time is

$$
T(n) = \Theta(n) + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} O(n_i^2), \qquad
\mathbb{E}[T(n)] = \Theta(n) + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} O\!\left(\mathbb{E}[n_i^2]\right).
$$

Now assume the $n$ keys are independent and uniform on the interval. Each key falls into bucket $i$ with probability $1/n$, independently, so $n_i$ is a binomial random variable with $n$ trials and success probability $p = 1/n$. Its mean is $np = 1$ and its variance is $np(1-p) = 1 - 1/n$, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = \operatorname{Var}[n_i] + \mathbb{E}[n_i]^2 = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right) + 1 = 2 - \frac{1}{n}.
$$ {#eq-lts-bucket}

Every one of the $n$ buckets contributes $O(2 - 1/n) = O(1)$, so $\mathbb{E}[T(n)] = \Theta(n) + n \cdot O(1) = \Theta(n)$ (this is the analysis of CLRS §8.4). The cell below checks @eq-lts-bucket empirically: the average of $\sum_i n_i^2$ over many uniform inputs should be close to $n(2 - 1/n) = 2n - 1$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-a4-demo
def a4_bucket(a, lo=0.0, hi=1.0):           # keys in [lo, hi)
    n = len(a)
    if n == 0:
        return []
    B = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for x in a:
        B[min(n - 1, int(n * (x - lo) / (hi - lo)))].append(x)
    out = []
    for b in B:
        for i in range(1, len(b)):          # insertion sort, as in CLRS
            x, j = b[i], i - 1
            while j >= 0 and b[j] > x:
                b[j + 1] = b[j]
                j -= 1
            b[j + 1] = x
        out += b
    return out

for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.uniform(-5.0, 7.0) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 60))]
    assert a4_bucket(arr, -5.0, 7.0) == sorted(arr)
assert a4_bucket([0.78, 0.17, 0.39, 0.26, 0.72, 0.94, 0.21, 0.12, 0.23, 0.68]) == \
    sorted([0.78, 0.17, 0.39, 0.26, 0.72, 0.94, 0.21, 0.12, 0.23, 0.68])

n_b, trials, total = 50, 2000, 0             # E[sum n_i^2] should be about 2n - 1 = 99
for _ in range(trials):
    sizes = Counter(int(n_b * random.random()) for _ in range(n_b))
    total += sum(c * c for c in sizes.values())
avg = total / trials
print(f"average sum of n_i^2 over {trials} uniform inputs: {avg:.2f} (theory {2 * n_b - 1})")
assert abs(avg - (2 * n_b - 1)) < 3

skew = [random.random() / 1000 for _ in range(n_b)]          # all keys in [0, 0.001)
assert max(Counter(int(n_b * x) for x in skew).values()) == n_b   # one bucket gets everything
print("a4 bucket OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// bucket sort of doubles in [lo, hi): n buckets, insertion sort inside each
vector<double> bucketSort(const vector<double>& a, double lo, double hi) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    vector<vector<double>> B(n);
    for (double x : a) B[min(n - 1, (int)(n * (x - lo) / (hi - lo)))].push_back(x);
    vector<double> out;
    out.reserve(n);
    for (auto& b : B) {
        for (size_t i = 1; i < b.size(); ++i) {           // insertion sort
            double x = b[i];
            int j = (int)i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && b[j] > x) { b[j + 1] = b[j]; --j; }
            b[j + 1] = x;
        }
        out.insert(out.end(), b.begin(), b.end());
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::

The last lines of the Python cell show the failure mode: squeeze every key into $[0, 0.001)$ and all $n$ land in bucket $0$, so the insertion sort there is $\Theta(n^2)$ in the worst case. Three ways to soften it: sort each bucket with an $O(m\log m)$ sort instead (worst case back to $O(n\log n)$), choose bucket boundaries from a sample of the data, or recognise that the input is not uniform and use another sort. The expectation is over the **input distribution**, not over random choices the algorithm makes; no coin flips inside the algorithm can rescue a bad input, unlike randomized quicksort.

The same picture, $n$ keys in $n$ equal-width buckets, powers arguments that never sort at all. In Maximum Gap (@sec-srt-p3-b) the averaging argument shows the answer is at least the bucket width, so only bucket minima and maxima matter; in @sec-lts-p5-b buckets of width $t + 1$ make "within $t$" a same-or-neighbour bucket question.

## A5. Value-as-index: the array stores its own counts {#sec-lts-a5}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
The most frugal use of "values are addresses": when the data is a permutation of $1..n$, or every value lies in $[1, n]$, you can **store information about value $v$ at index $v-1$** of the input array itself, with no separate histogram. Mark a slot by **negating** it to record "I have seen this value," or **swap each value into its home index** (cyclic placement) so the array becomes its own presence table. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space. This is what "could you do it without extra space?" is quietly asking for.
:::

Counting sort with $k = n$ needs an $n$-cell count array. When the input already *is* an $n$-cell array whose values are in $[1, n]$, it can double as that count array, as long as we can store a little extra information in each cell without losing the value that lives there. Sign marking borrows one bit per cell (the sign), which is enough to record "seen / not seen". Cyclic placement instead moves each value to its home, so cell $i$ either holds $i + 1$ or names a gap. Both rely on the value range being $[1, n]$; step outside it and every index must be guarded. @sec-idx develops these index tricks further (permutation cycles, marking in matrices); this chapter uses them only as the zero-space limit of counting.

```text
sign_mark(a):                               # values in 1..n
    for x in a:
        i = abs(x) - 1
        if a[i] > 0: a[i] = -a[i]           # mark slot i as "seen value i+1"
    # now a[i] < 0 <=> value i+1 occurred

cyclic_place(a):                            # place v at index v-1
    for i: while 1<=a[i]<=n and a[a[i]-1] != a[i]: swap a[i] with a[a[i]-1]
```

::: {#fig-lts-a5}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def a5_draw(ax, p):
    data = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]
    marked = list(data)                       # sign marking, computed inline for the figure
    for x in data:
        i = abs(x) - 1
        if marked[i] > 0:
            marked[i] = -marked[i]
    assert [i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(marked) if v > 0] == [5, 6]
    V.trace(ax, p, [
        dict(values=data, label="values in 1..8", note="index i stands for value i+1",
             colors={i: "muted" for i in range(len(data))}),
        dict(values=marked, label="after marking", note="slot i negative iff value i+1 seen",
             colors={i: ("green" if marked[i] < 0 else "amber") for i in range(len(data))}),
    ], gap=2.6)
V.show(a5_draw)
```

$[4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1]$: the values 5 and 6 never occur, so slots 4 and 5 keep their positive sign. Reading "still positive means missing" gives $[5,6]$, which is @sec-lts-p2-a, with no extra array.

:::

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-a5-demo
def a5_sign(a):                             # values in 1..n; returns a marked copy
    a = list(a)
    for x in a:
        i = abs(x) - 1
        if a[i] > 0:
            a[i] = -a[i]
    return a

def a5_cyclic(a):                           # place v at index v-1, return the rearranged copy
    a = list(a)
    n = len(a)
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = a[i] - 1
        if 1 <= a[i] <= n and a[j] != a[i]:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
        else:
            i += 1
    return a

assert [abs(v) for v in a5_sign([4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1])] == [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]
assert [i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(a5_sign([4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1])) if v > 0] == [5, 6]
for _ in range(300):
    perm = list(range(1, random.randint(1, 12) + 1))
    random.shuffle(perm)
    assert a5_cyclic(perm) == sorted(perm)  # a permutation of 1..n sorts completely, in O(n)
assert a5_cyclic([1, 1]) == [1, 1]
print("a5 value-as-index OK")
```

The first assertion checks that marking keeps every magnitude, so the values are not lost. The stress loop shows that cyclic placement **sorts** a permutation of $1..n$ in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space: it is counting sort for the special case where every count is exactly one. The guard `1 <= a[i] <= n` is the difference between a clean permutation (@sec-lts-p2-a, @sec-lts-p5-a) and an array of arbitrary integers (@sec-lts-p2-b), where only the in-range values get placed.

## A6. When values beat comparisons, and the pigeonhole {#sec-lts-a6}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Three closing ideas. **(1) The decision.** A linear-time sort is a bet on the keys: counting sort needs a small integer range ($k = O(n)$), radix sort needs keys made of a few small digits, bucket sort needs a known interval and a near-uniform spread. If none holds, use a comparison sort from @sec-salgo. **(2) The pigeonhole.** $n$ items in fewer than $n$ boxes force two items into one box; phrased over value ranges instead of array slots, this solves @sec-lts-p5-a and @sec-lts-p5-b. **(3) Histograms as equality tests.** To decide "same multiset?" without sorting, compare counts: @sec-lts-p4-b.
:::

Read the constraints as a menu. If they *promise* small integer values, a bounded alphabet, or fixed-width keys, you are being invited off the comparison wall; if they only bound $n$ and say "any integers", sort (or select) with the tools of @sec-salgo. Even then, remember **coordinate compression** (@sec-srt-a4): sorting once to replace values by their ranks $0..n-1$ turns any later counting step into a small-range one.

::: {#fig-lts-a6}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def a6_draw(ax, p):
    V.flow(ax, p, {
        "small": (0.0, 1.6, "integer keys, range k = O(n): counting sort", "amber"),
        "tuple": (0.0, 0.2, "d small digits in base b: radix sort", "indigo"),
        "unif":  (0.0, -1.2, "reals, uniform on an interval: bucket sort", "cyan"),
        "none":  (0.0, -2.6, "no promise about the keys: comparison sort", "green"),
    }, [("small", "tuple", ""), ("tuple", "unif", ""), ("unif", "none", "")], w=10.5, h=0.7)
V.show(a6_draw)
```

Walk down the ladder and take the first rung whose assumption you can *verify from the statement*: counting sort costs $O(n + k)$, radix sort $O(d(n + b))$, bucket sort expected $O(n)$. If you reach the bottom rung, call an $O(n\log n)$ comparison sort.

:::

| | Counting sort | LSD radix sort | Bucket sort | Comparison sorts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Keys | integers in a range of size $k$ | $d$ digits in base $b$ | reals in a known interval | anything with `<` |
| Time | $\Theta(n + k)$ | $\Theta(d(n + b))$ | expected $\Theta(n)$ if uniform; worst $\Theta(n^2)$ with insertion sort | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |
| Extra space | $\Theta(n + k)$ | $\Theta(n + b)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | $O(1)$ to $O(n)$ |
| Stable | yes (A2 form) | yes | yes, with a stable inner sort | depends (@sec-salgo) |
| Breaks when | $k \gg n$ | many or wide digits | keys bunch together | never; the safe default |

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-a6-demo
# the pigeonhole: n balls in m boxes force some box to hold at least ceil(n / m)
def a6_max_box_lower_bound(n, m):
    return -(-n // m)

for _ in range(300):
    n, m = random.randint(1, 30), random.randint(1, 10)
    boxes = Counter(random.randrange(m) for _ in range(n))
    assert max(boxes.values()) >= a6_max_box_lower_bound(n, m)   # holds for every placement
assert a6_max_box_lower_bound(10, 3) == 4
assert a6_max_box_lower_bound(9, 8) == 2     # 9 values from a range of size 8: a repeat is forced

# histogram equality decides "same multiset" without sorting (@sec-lts-p4-b)
def a6_hist_eq(s, t):
    if len(s) != len(t):
        return False
    cnt = [0] * 26
    for a, b in zip(s, t):
        cnt[ord(a) - 97] += 1
        cnt[ord(b) - 97] -= 1
    return all(c == 0 for c in cnt)

assert a6_hist_eq("listen", "silent") is True and a6_hist_eq("listen", "silens") is False
print("a6 pigeonhole + histogram-equality OK")
```

The first block is the pigeonhole principle in its counting form: every random placement of $n$ balls in $m$ boxes has a box with at least $\lceil n/m \rceil$ balls. With $n = m + 1$ that is "some box holds two", which is the repeat that @sec-lts-p5-a reads off. The second block is @sec-lts-p4-b in a few lines.

## Part B — Patterns

Part B uses the lessons on real problems. Each pattern opens with the signals that say "use me", a boxed template with its invariant, and its complexity, then at least two fully solved problems with a brute force, the refined solution, matching C++, and a stress test against the brute force.

## Pattern 1: Sort when the value range is small {#sec-lts-p1}

**Where we are.** A1 to A6 built the tools; Part B spends them, one idea per pattern. P1 is the plainest case: the statement hands you a small integer key, and a histogram replaces the sort. P2 makes the value an index into the *input array itself*, for $O(1)$ space. P3 makes the *frequency* the index, so "sort by how often" needs no comparisons. P4 uses the key as an address to answer a question (rebuild an order, test equality) without sorting at all. P5 uses value-range boxes so tight that a collision *is* the answer. P6 removes the one condition all of these need, a small range: a wide key is split into small digits and sorted digit by digit with radix sort.

**Recognise it.** The constraint reads $1 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 100$, or $\le n$, or the key is a letter or a digit. Also: values may be large, but anything above some bound $B \le n$ behaves the same (clamp it). These say *the value range is the budget*, which is counting sort's ticket.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Trade the $\log n$ comparison factor for a $k$-wide array.

```text
histogram:  cnt[v] += 1 over the input (clamp v to a bound if larger values act alike)
read:       walk v = 0..k-1 (or k-1..0), using cnt[v] or its running sum
```

**Invariant.** After the tally, `cnt[v]` is the number of items with key $v$, and the running sum $\sum_{u < v} \mathit{cnt}[u]$ is the first position key $v$ would occupy in sorted order. Reading the indices in order reproduces the sorted array, or any count over it, without a single comparison.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n + k)$ time, $O(k)$ space, linear whenever $k = O(n)$. The comparison sort being replaced is $O(n\log n)$; the gain is the deleted $\log n$, the price the $k$-wide array.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1051-height-checker/problem.qmd >}}

[**From one upward read to reading back and forth.** Height Checker reads its histogram once, low to high. Increasing Decreasing String reads the same kind of 26-slot histogram up, then down, again and again, taking one item per slot per sweep.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1370-increasing-decreasing-string/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a small alphabet to a clamped range.** Both problems so far had keys that were small to begin with. H-Index has citation counts up to $1000$, but no count above $n$ can matter, so clamping squeezes the keys into $[0, n]$; the histogram is then read from the top with a running sum.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0274-h-index/problem.qmd >}}

[**From reading the counts to reading the block boundaries.** H-Index used running sums of the histogram as a count of papers. AquaMoon uses the same running sums as A2 does, as the **positions** where each value's block starts in sorted order, and checks a parity condition on every block without building the sorted array.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1545a-aquamoon-and-strange-sort/problem.qmd >}}

One more problem of this pattern is solved in full in @sec-srt, where counting sort first appeared as a tool: Relative Sort Array emits a histogram in a custom order (the order of a second array, then the leftovers ascending).

{{< include ../problems/lc-1122-relative-sort-array/card.qmd >}}

## Pattern 2: Turn the value into an index {#sec-lts-p2}

**From an auxiliary histogram to the array's own slots.** Pattern 1 paid $O(k)$ for a separate count array. When the values *are* $1..n$ (a permutation, or "each value in range"), the input array already has one slot per possible value, so store the information there and drop to $O(1)$ extra space. Sign marking borrows a bit; cyclic placement moves each value home. This is A5: counting sort with the histogram folded into the input.

**Recognise it.** "Values are in $[1, n]$" or "a permutation of $1..n$", plus the follow-up *"without extra space"* (or "$O(1)$ auxiliary space").

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Index the array by value $- 1$ and let the slot record "seen" (or hold its owner).

```text
sign:   i = abs(x)-1; if a[i] > 0: a[i] = -a[i]          # negative slot => value i+1 seen
cyclic: while 1<=a[i]<=n and a[a[i]-1] != a[i]: swap a[i], a[a[i]-1]   # send a[i] home
```

**Invariant.** With sign marking, slot $i$ is negative iff value $i+1$ occurred; with cyclic placement, every in-range value ends at its own index, so `a[i] != i+1` marks a missing value.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space for both (mutating the input or a copy). The hash-set alternative is $O(n)$ space: the oracle, and exactly what the constraint forbids.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0448-find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From "which slots stayed positive" to "send every value home".** LC 448 marks seen values and reads the untouched slots. LC 41 must cope with values outside $[1, n]$ (negatives, zero, huge numbers), so it guards the index and places each in-range value at its home instead.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0041-first-missing-positive/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 3: Let the frequency be the bucket {#sec-lts-p3}

**From value buckets to count buckets.** Patterns 1 and 2 indexed by the *value*. Many problems sort by a *derived* small integer instead: how often something appears. A count is also a valid array index, in $[1, n]$. Drop each item into `buckets[frequency]` and scan down: that is a counting sort whose key is the count, and it compares nothing.

**Recognise it.** "Sort by frequency", "the $k$ most frequent", any tie order accepted, $n$ up to $10^5$, and a follow-up asking for better than $O(n\log n)$.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Two stages of counting: value → frequency, then frequency → bucket index.

```text
c = Counter(items)
buckets = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
for x, f in c.items(): buckets[f].append(x)
scan f = n..1 (collect; optionally stop after k items)
```

**Invariant.** An item sits only in the bucket equal to its frequency, so a downward scan visits items in non-increasing frequency, exactly the required order, in $O(n + A)$.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n + A)$ time, $O(n)$ space ($A$ = number of distinct items). Sorting the distinct items by count is the $O(n + A\log A)$ oracle; the buckets delete the $\log$.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0451-sort-characters-by-frequency/problem.qmd >}}

[**From emitting every bucket to stopping at $k$.** LC 451 walks all frequency buckets to rebuild the whole string. LC 347 uses the same buckets but stops once $k$ values are collected: the same count-as-index structure with an early exit, $O(n)$ where `most_common` is $O(n + A\log A)$.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0347-top-k-frequent-elements/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 4: Positional and histogram equality {#sec-lts-p4}

**From sorting to answering.** Sometimes no order is needed in the output at all. Either the data already carries each item's destination and the only job is to write it there (@sec-lts-p4-a), or the question is just whether two multisets are equal (@sec-lts-p4-b). The first is the placement phase of counting sort with the positions handed over; the second is its counting phase used as an equality test.

**Recognise it.** "Each item carries its own position" → direct placement. "Are these the same multiset / anagrams?" → compare counts, never sort.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Use the key as an address to write, or as an address to tally.

```text
place:  out[key - 1] = payload                     # the embedded index IS the slot (A1, A2)
equal:  one counter, += for A, -= for B; equal iff every slot is 0   (A6)
```

**Invariant.** If the keys form a permutation of $1..n$, direct placement fills every slot exactly once; a shared histogram nets to zero iff the two multisets are identical.
:::

**Complexity.** Both $O(n)$ time; placement uses $O(n)$ space for the output, the equality test $O(1)$ (fixed alphabet) or $O(A)$ for a general alphabet. Sorting both is the $O(n\log n)$ fallback.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1859-sorting-the-sentence/problem.qmd >}}

[**From writing at an index to tallying at an index.** LC 1859 uses each word's digit as an address to *place* the word. LC 242 uses each character as an address to *count*, turning "is this an anagram?" into "does the histogram net to zero?".]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0242-valid-anagram/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 5: The value-range pigeonhole {#sec-lts-p5}

**From one box per value to a forced collision.** A4 scattered keys into equal-width buckets; A6 named the consequence: more items than boxes, and some box repeats. When the value range is no larger than the number of items, a collision is guaranteed, and the problem is to read *which* box collided (@sec-lts-p5-a), or to choose boxes so tight that "within $t$" becomes "same or adjacent box" (@sec-lts-p5-b). This is the pattern where the counting argument matters more than any sorting.

**Recognise it.** "Values in $[1, n]$ with exactly one repeated and one missing" (a permutation with one defect). Or "two values within $t$ of each other, at indices within $k$": the bucket-of-width-$t{+}1$ signal. Or "maximum gap between neighbours in sorted order, in linear time": buckets plus an averaging argument.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Choose the boxes so that the promise forces the answer.

```text
defect:  mark slot abs(x)-1; a second hit = duplicate, an untouched slot = missing   (A5)
close:   bucket width t+1; a hit in the same bucket, or a close value in a neighbour,
         among the last k items, is the pair                                          (A4)
```

**Invariant.** Negated slots record occurrence, so the doubled box and the empty box are readable afterwards. With width-$(t+1)$ buckets, two values within $t$ share a bucket or sit in neighbouring buckets, and two values in one bucket are always within $t$, so three probes per item suffice.
:::

**Complexity.** The defect read is $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space. The bucket window is $O(n)$ expected time, $O(\min(n, k))$ space; an ordered-set window is $O(n\log k)$ worst case.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0645-set-mismatch/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a permutation with one defect to a window over a value range.** LC 645 reads the pigeonhole's doubled and empty boxes on a nearly valid $1..n$ set. LC 220 makes the boxes value ranges of width $t+1$ and adds an index window, so the same "boxes force the answer" reasoning becomes a linear-time test for a close pair.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0220-contains-duplicate-iii/problem.qmd >}}

The third member of this pattern, Maximum Gap, is solved in full in @sec-srt: $n$ keys in $n - 1$ equal buckets, an averaging argument that puts the answer *between* buckets, and only per-bucket minima and maxima kept. It can also be solved by radix-sorting the keys (Pattern 6) and scanning neighbours, since the keys are integers up to $10^9$.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0164-maximum-gap/card.qmd >}}

## Pattern 6: Radix sort: split a wide key into small digits {#sec-lts-p6}

**From a small range to any fixed-width key.** Every pattern so far needed a small range: a histogram of $k$ cells is only cheap when $k$ is about $n$ or smaller. Radix sort (A3) removes that need. A 32-bit integer is four 8-bit digits; a string of length $m$ is $m$ letters. Run one stable counting sort per digit, least significant first, and a wide key costs $d$ cheap passes instead of one impossible histogram. Two twists recur in problems: the digits may each need their own direction, and the order after *some* of the passes may itself be an answer.

**Recognise it.** Keys of a fixed, short width: equal-length strings, digit strings, integers with a known bit count, tuples like (year, month, day). A custom order defined position by position ("compare the first differing character, ascending at odd positions"). Queries that ask about the order of *suffixes* of the keys (the last $t$ digits).

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
One stable counting sort per digit, least significant first; map each digit so that the pass is ascending.

```text
order = [0, 1, ..., n-1]                        # sort indices, not the keys themselves
for column j = last .. first:
    digit(i) = key[i][j]   (or  R-1-key[i][j]   if this column sorts descending)
    order = stable_counting_sort(order, digit)  # O(n + R)
    # here: order is sorted by columns j..last  (save it if a query needs it)
```

**Invariant.** After the passes on columns $j..m$, `order` is sorted by those columns, and keys equal on them are in their original (index) order. Each new pass extends this by one column to the left because it is stable (@sec-lts-a3-proof).
:::

**Complexity.** $O(m(n + R))$ time for $n$ keys of $m$ digits over an alphabet of size $R$, $O(n + R)$ extra space; linear in the input size $nm$ when $R = O(n)$. A comparison sort costs $O(nm\log n)$ in the worst case, since each comparison may read $m$ digits.

{{< include ../problems/cf-1575a-another-sorting-problem/problem.qmd >}}

[**From the final order to every intermediate order.** In Another Sorting Problem only the order after the last pass matters. In Query Kth Smallest Trimmed Number the order after pass $t$ answers every query with trim $t$, and the tie rule "lower index first" comes free from stability.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-2343-query-kth-smallest-trimmed-number/problem.qmd >}}

Radix sort is also a guaranteed-linear way to answer Distinct Numbers, solved with a hash set in @sec-hash: radix-sort the values (up to $10^9$, so two passes of 16-bit digits) and count the positions where a value differs from its left neighbour.

{{< include ../problems/cses-1621-distinct-numbers/card.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** Every pattern traded comparisons for something the constraints said about the keys. Counting sort (A1, A2) spends a $k$-wide array to sort small integer keys (P1), and its counting half alone answers equality and placement questions (P4). Value-as-index (A5) folds that array into the input for $O(1)$ space (P2). Frequency buckets apply counting sort to a derived key, the count (P3). Equal-width buckets (A4) need no order at all when the pigeonhole forces the answer (P5). And radix sort (A3) stretches all of this to wide keys by running the stable counting sort once per digit (P6). The thread is a single licence: the keys told you something, so you indexed with them instead of comparing them.

## Pattern map

<!-- Copied into the Cheat Sheets appendix by gen_book.py: keep it one table, no labels. -->

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Values bounded by a small constant ($\le 100$, a letter); compare with the sorted order | Histogram, read by index | @sec-lts-p1-a |
| Repeatedly take smallest/largest remaining over a fixed alphabet | Re-read a histogram up and down | @sec-lts-p1-b |
| Values large, but anything above $n$ acts the same | Clamp to $n$, read from the top with a running sum | @sec-lts-p1-c |
| A condition on each value's block in sorted order | Prefix sums of the histogram = block starts | @sec-lts-p1-d |
| "Values are $1..n$", "without extra space", find the vanished values | Sign marking as the counter | @sec-lts-p2-a |
| Smallest missing positive, arbitrary integers, $O(1)$ space | Cyclic placement at index $v-1$ | @sec-lts-p2-b |
| "Sort by frequency", whole result emitted | Frequency as bucket index | @sec-lts-p3-a |
| "Top $k$ frequent", linear time | Frequency buckets with early exit | @sec-lts-p3-b |
| Each item carries its own destination index | Direct placement (the key is an address) | @sec-lts-p4-a |
| "Same multiset?" / anagram | One shared histogram nets to zero | @sec-lts-p4-b |
| A permutation of $1..n$ with one duplicate and one loss | Pigeonhole with sign marking | @sec-lts-p5-a |
| Two values within $t$ at indices within $k$ | Buckets of width $t+1$, probe neighbours | @sec-lts-p5-b |
| Equal-length strings, custom per-position order | LSD radix, one stable pass per column | @sec-lts-p6-a |
| Queries about the order of the last $t$ digits | LSD radix, keep the order after each pass | @sec-lts-p6-b |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Counting sort on a wide range.** $O(n + k)$ is linear only when $k = O(n)$. If values reach $10^9$, the count array has $10^9$ cells: clamp (@sec-lts-p1-c), compress to ranks (@sec-srt-a4), radix-sort (@sec-lts-a3), or use a comparison sort (@sec-lts-a1, @sec-lts-a6).
- **End positions with a forward scan.** With $C[v]$ = "number of keys $\le v$" you must place from the back; with $C[v]$ = "first slot of $v$" you must place from the front. Mixing them reverses every group of equal keys, and a radix sort built on it gives wrong answers (@sec-lts-a2).
- **LSD passes in the wrong order, or an unstable pass.** LSD radix must go from the least to the most significant digit with a *stable* inner sort; either mistake lets a later pass destroy the order the earlier ones built (@sec-lts-a3-proof).
- **Negative keys in radix sort.** `(x // exp) % 10` and `(x >> s) & 255` do not order negative numbers correctly. Offset by the minimum or flip the sign bit first (@sec-lts-a3-neg).
- **LSD on strings of different lengths.** There is no common last column; padding is expensive. Use MSD radix sort, or bucket by length first (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
- **Forgetting the "ended" bucket in MSD.** A string that runs out of characters must sort *before* every longer string with the same prefix; it needs its own bucket, smaller than every character (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
- **Bucket sort on data you have not checked.** Skewed keys pile into one bucket, and the inner insertion sort becomes $\Theta(n^2)$ (@sec-lts-a4-proof).
- **Indexing by value without guarding the range.** `a[x - 1]` is safe only when $1 \le x \le n$; LC 41's negatives and huge values must be skipped (@sec-lts-a5, @sec-lts-p2-b).
- **Forgetting the absolute value in sign marking.** Once slots are negated, later reads must use `abs(x) - 1` (@sec-lts-p2-a, @sec-lts-p5-a).
- **Cyclic placement on duplicates without the home check.** Without `a[a[i]-1] != a[i]`, two equal values swap forever (@sec-lts-p2-b).
- **Truncating division for bucket ids.** In C++ `-1 / 2 == 0`, the same bucket as `1 / 2`; bucket ids of negative values need a real floor (@sec-lts-p5-b).
- **Sorting to answer an equality question.** "Are these anagrams?" needs counts, not an order: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space instead of $O(n\log n)$ (@sec-lts-p4-b).
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E] Trace stable counting sort (count, prefix sums, backward placement) on $A = [6, 0, 2, 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 1, 3, 2]$ with $k = 7$. Give $C$ after the count pass and after the prefix pass, and the final output.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Counts of $0..6$: $C = [2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 0, 2]$. Prefix sums: $C = [2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 9, 11]$. Placing from the back gives $B = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 6]$. For example, the last key $2$ (index 10) goes to slot $C[2] - 1 = 5$, and the earlier $2$ (index 2) later goes to slot $4$, so the two 2s keep their input order (@sec-lts-a2).

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-ex1
ex1 = [6, 0, 2, 0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 1, 3, 2]
assert [ex1.count(v) for v in range(7)] == [2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 0, 2]
assert list(np.cumsum([ex1.count(v) for v in range(7)])) == [2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 9, 11]
assert a2_stable(ex1, key=lambda x: x) == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 6, 6]
```
:::

**2. [E] Counting sort is said to run in $O(n + k)$. What exactly is $k$, and give an input on which counting sort is asymptotically worse than merge sort.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$k$ is the size of the key **range** (the number of cells in the count array), $\max - \min + 1$ after shifting. With $n = 10$ keys spread up to $10^9$, counting sort allocates and scans $10^9$ cells, while merge sort does about $10 \log_2 10 \approx 33$ comparisons. Counting sort wins only when $k = O(n)$ or smaller (@sec-lts-a1).
:::

**3. [E] In the A2 placement loop, replace the backward scan by a forward scan but keep $C[v]$ = "number of keys $\le v$" and the decrement. Is the result still sorted? Is it stable? Show it on `(2,a), (1,b), (2,c)`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Still sorted: every record still lands inside its key's block. Not stable: the forward scan meets `(2,a)` first and gives it the **last** slot of the key-2 block, so ties come out reversed. Here $C = [0, 1, 3]$ after the prefix pass; forward placement puts `(2,a)` in slot 2, `(1,b)` in slot 0, `(2,c)` in slot 1, giving `b, c, a` instead of the stable `b, a, c` (@sec-lts-a2).
:::

**4. [M] Prove that the LSD radix sort of @sec-lts-a3 is wrong if the passes go from the most significant digit to the least significant, each pass being a stable sort of the whole array. Give a two-element counterexample.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With the passes reversed, the **last** pass sorts by the least significant digit, so the final order is by the units digit, with ties broken by the higher digits. For $[19, 21]$: the tens pass gives $[19, 21]$, then the units pass sorts by $9$ and $1$ and gives $[21, 19]$, which is wrong. The proof in @sec-lts-a3-proof needs the newest pass to be the most significant so far (@sec-lts-a3).
:::

**5. [M] Radix-sort $[329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355]$ in base 10 by hand. After which pass is the array first fully sorted, and why can it not be earlier in general?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Units pass: $720, 355, 436, 457, 657, 329, 839$. Tens pass: $720, 329, 436, 839, 355, 457, 657$. Hundreds pass: $329, 355, 436, 457, 657, 720, 839$. The array is sorted only after the hundreds pass: after $j$ passes it is sorted by the lowest $j$ digits only, and two keys that differ only in the highest digit can be in any order before the last pass (@fig-lts-anim-radix).
:::

**6. [M] Show how to sort $n$ integers in the range $[0, n^3 - 1]$ in $O(n)$ time.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write each integer in base $n$: since it is below $n^3$, it has at most three base-$n$ digits, each in $[0, n-1]$. Run LSD radix sort with $b = n$ and $d = 3$: $\Theta(3(n + n)) = \Theta(n)$. Counting sort directly would cost $\Theta(n + n^3)$ (@sec-lts-a3-base).

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-ex6
for _ in range(100):
    n6 = random.randint(1, 30)
    arr6 = [random.randrange(n6 ** 3) for _ in range(n6)]
    assert a3_radix(arr6, base=max(2, n6)) == sorted(arr6)
```
:::

**7. [M] You must sort $10^6$ unsigned 64-bit keys with LSD radix sort. Using @eq-lts-radix-r, compare digits of 8, 16 and 22 bits.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$r = 8$: 8 passes of $n + 256$, about $8.0 \cdot 10^6$ steps. $r = 16$: 4 passes of $n + 65536$, about $4.3 \cdot 10^6$. $r = 22$: 3 passes of $n + 4.2 \cdot 10^6$, about $15.6 \cdot 10^6$. So 16-bit digits minimise the step count; 8-bit digits are often preferred in practice because a 256-entry count array stays in the fastest cache (@sec-lts-a3-base).
:::

**8. [M] Explain why flipping the sign bit (`x ^ 0x80000000`) makes 32-bit signed integers radix-sortable as unsigned, and why an offset by the minimum is an alternative.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In two's complement, $x$ and $x + 2^{32}$ have the same bit pattern, so reading signed $x$ as unsigned gives $x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $x + 2^{32}$ for $x < 0$: negatives look larger than positives. Flipping the top bit adds $2^{31}$ modulo $2^{32}$, which maps $[-2^{31}, 2^{31})$ onto $[0, 2^{32})$ by $x \mapsto x + 2^{31}$, an increasing map. An offset by $-\min$ is the same idea with the smallest shift that makes every key non-negative (@sec-lts-a3-neg).
:::

**9. [M] Trace MSD radix sort on `["dab", "cab", "ad", "add", "dad", "a"]`. Which groups are recursed into, and at what depth?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Depth 0 by the first letter: `a` group `[ad, add, a]`, `c` group `[cab]`, `d` group `[dab, dad]`. Recurse into `a` at depth 1: `a` has ended (bucket 0), `ad` and `add` go to bucket `d`, so the order is `a, ad, add` after recursing into `[ad, add]` at depth 2 (`ad` ended, `add` has `d`). Recurse into `d` at depth 1: both have `a`, recurse at depth 2: `dab` (`b`) before `dad` (`d`). Result: `a, ad, add, cab, dab, dad` (@sec-lts-a3-msd).

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-ex9
assert a3_msd(["dab", "cab", "ad", "add", "dad", "a"]) == ["a", "ad", "add", "cab", "dab", "dad"]
```
:::

**10. [M] Why does MSD radix sort not need its counting passes to be stable for correctness, while LSD does?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
MSD never re-sorts keys that an earlier pass has already separated: after the pass on character $d$, each group shares the first $d + 1$ characters, and later passes work only inside one group. So no later pass can undo an earlier decision, and ties inside the last pass are equal strings. LSD re-sorts the *whole* array every pass, and only stability protects the order fixed by the lower digits (@sec-lts-a3-proof, @sec-lts-a3-msd).
:::

**11. [M] Bucket sort over $[0, 1)$ is expected $O(n)$ for uniform input. Give an input on which it takes $\Theta(n^2)$, and change one line so the worst case becomes $O(n\log n)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Put all keys in $[0, 1/n)$ in decreasing order: they all land in bucket 0 in reverse order, and insertion sort there does $\Theta(n^2)$ shifts. Sorting each bucket with merge sort (or Python's `sorted`) instead of insertion sort bounds the work by $O(n\log n)$ while keeping the expected $O(n)$ on uniform input (@sec-lts-a4-proof).
:::

**12. [H] Bucket sort with $m$ buckets instead of $n$: show that the expected time is $\Theta(n + n^2/m + m)$ for uniform input.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Now $n_i$ is binomial with $p = 1/m$: $\mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = np(1-p) + (np)^2 = n/m - n/m^2 + n^2/m^2$. Summing over $m$ buckets: $\sum_i \mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = n - n/m + n^2/m = \Theta(n + n^2/m)$. Add $\Theta(n + m)$ for scattering and scanning the buckets: $\Theta(n + n^2/m + m)$, minimised at $m = \Theta(n)$, where it is $\Theta(n)$ (@eq-lts-bucket).
:::

**13. [E] For values $1..n$ with some missing, sign marking finds the gaps in $O(1)$ extra space. Why must every value be in $[1, n]$, and how does @sec-lts-p2-b work around negatives and huge values?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The mark is written at index `abs(x) - 1`, so $x$ must name one of the $n$ slots; anything else indexes out of bounds. LC 41 skips every $x \notin [1, n]$ (guard `1 <= a[i] <= n`): the answer is always in $[1, n+1]$, so only in-range values can affect it (@sec-lts-a5, @sec-lts-p2-b).
:::

**14. [M] In @sec-lts-p2-b the inner loop is a `while` (not an `if`) and tests `a[a[i]-1] != a[i]`. Explain each choice, and bound the total number of swaps.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`while`: the value swapped *into* slot $i$ may itself belong elsewhere, so slot $i$ is processed until it holds its own value or a value that cannot be placed. The test: if the home slot already holds an equal value (a duplicate), a swap would change nothing and loop forever. Every successful swap puts one value into its home for good, so there are at most $n$ swaps in total and the whole loop is $O(n)$ (@sec-lts-p2-b).
:::

**15. [M] @sec-lts-p3-a sorts characters by frequency with buckets. Why are $n + 1$ buckets enough, and why does the stress test sort inside each bucket?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
No character occurs more than $n$ times, so every frequency is an index in $[1, n]$. Characters with equal frequency share a bucket and may come out in any order; the problem accepts that, but the stress test compares two programs' strings exactly, so sorting inside a bucket makes the output deterministic and the comparison meaningful (@sec-lts-p3-a).
:::

**16. [E] Give the $O(n)$-time, $O(1)$-space anagram test and explain why the length check comes first.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
One 26-slot array: `+= 1` for each character of `s`, `-= 1` for each of `t`, anagrams iff all slots are zero. The single loop walks `zip(s, t)`, which stops at the shorter string; without the length check, `s = "ab"`, `t = "abc"` would net to zero over the common prefix and wrongly pass (@sec-lts-p4-b).
:::

**17. [M] In @sec-lts-p5-a, why must the missing value be found by scanning the *slots* after the marking pass, while the duplicate is found during the pass?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The duplicate appears in the array twice, so the walk steps on its slot twice and sees the mark the second time. The missing value never appears, so nothing in the walk points to its slot; only a separate scan of all $n$ slots finds the one still unmarked (the pigeonhole's empty box) (@sec-lts-p5-a).
:::

**18. [H] In @sec-lts-p5-b, with bucket width $w = t + 1$, prove that two values within $t$ lie in the same or adjacent buckets, and that two values in the same bucket are within $t$. Why does that let the map hold one value per bucket?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Bucket $b$ holds exactly the integers in $[bw, bw + w - 1]$. Two values in it differ by at most $w - 1 = t$. If $|x - y| \le t < w$, then $\lfloor x/w \rfloor$ and $\lfloor y/w \rfloor$ differ by at most one. So among live elements, a second value in an occupied bucket would already be a valid pair and the scan would have stopped; while it runs, every bucket holds at most one live value, and the map can store that value directly (@sec-lts-p5-b).
:::

**19. [M] Sort $n$ student records by `(grade, score)` where grade $\in \{1..5\}$ and score $\in \{0..100\}$, grade first. Which passes do you run, in which order, and what does it cost? What changes if the score is an arbitrary real number?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
LSD order: first a stable counting sort by the **minor** key, score ($k = 101$), then a stable counting sort by the **major** key, grade ($k = 5$). Total $O(n + 101 + n + 5) = O(n)$. If the score is an arbitrary real, it cannot index an array; sort by score with a stable comparison sort ($O(n\log n)$), then the grade pass can still be a stable counting sort, or simply sort by the tuple key with a comparison sort (@sec-lts-a2, @sec-lts-a3).
:::

**20. [H] Explain, in terms of the decision-tree argument, why counting sort is not bound by $\Omega(n\log n)$, and name the resource it spends instead.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The bound models an algorithm as a binary tree whose internal nodes are comparisons; with $n!$ reachable leaves its height is at least $\log_2(n!)$ (@eq-lts-lower). Counting sort's basic step `cnt[x] += 1` uses the key as an address, which picks one of $k$ cells: a $k$-way branch on the key's value, not a two-way comparison, so the algorithm is not such a tree. It spends **memory proportional to the key range** and relies on the word-RAM ability to index by a key in $O(1)$; with $k = O(n)$ that buys $O(n)$ time (@sec-lts-a1-wall).
:::

**21. [M] Strings of total length $N$ over an alphabet of size $R$, of varying lengths. Compare: a comparison sort, LSD with padding to the longest length $w$, and MSD.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A comparison sort does $O(n\log n)$ comparisons, each of which may read many characters (up to the common prefix length). LSD with padding costs $\Theta(w(n + R))$, which can be far more than $N$: one string of length $10^5$ among $10^5$ short ones makes $w n = 10^{10}$. MSD reads only the distinguishing prefixes, at most $N$ characters, plus an $O(R)$ count array per recursive call, which is why practical MSD switches to insertion sort for small groups (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
:::

## Interview questions

<!-- Copied into the Question Bank (quiz mode) by gen_book.py. Keep the shape exactly: a bold line
     starting "**N. " with the question, then one collapsed "Answer" callout. Answers may cite @sec-… -->

**1. What does the $\Omega(n\log n)$ sorting lower bound assume, and how does counting sort get around it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It assumes the algorithm learns about the order **only by comparing pairs of keys**; then a decision tree with $n!$ leaves has height at least $\log_2(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$. Counting sort never compares: it uses each key as an array index, a step with $k$ outcomes, so the argument does not apply. It runs in $O(n + k)$, linear when the key range $k$ is $O(n)$ (@sec-lts-a1-wall).
:::

**2. When is counting sort a bad idea even though it is "linear"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When the key range $k$ is much larger than $n$: keys up to $10^9$ need a $10^9$-cell array, worse than $O(n\log n)$ in time and memory. Also when the keys are not integers (or cannot be mapped to small integers). Check the value range in the constraints first; consider clamping, coordinate compression or radix sort (@sec-lts-a1, @sec-lts-a6).
:::

**3. What does "stable" mean, and how does counting sort achieve it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A stable sort keeps records with equal keys in their input order. Counting sort turns counts into end positions with a prefix sum and then places records scanning **backward**, decrementing the position; equal keys fill their block from the right in reverse input order, so they end up in input order. (Equivalently: start positions with a forward scan.) (@sec-lts-a2).
:::

**4. Walk through LSD radix sort and explain why the per-digit sort must be stable.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sort by the units digit, then the tens, then the hundreds, each time with a stable counting sort. After $j$ passes the array is sorted by the lowest $j$ digits. When the next pass meets two keys with the same digit, only stability keeps them in the order the lower digits established; an unstable pass could swap them and break the result (@sec-lts-a3-proof).
:::

**5. Counting sort or radix sort for $n$ integers in $[0, n^2)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Radix sort. Counting sort would be $\Theta(n + n^2)$. Each key has two base-$n$ digits, so two stable counting-sort passes with $b = n$ cost $\Theta(2(n + n)) = \Theta(n)$ (@sec-lts-a3-base).
:::

**6. How do you pick the digit size for radix sort?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For $\beta$-bit keys and $r$-bit digits the cost is $\Theta((\beta/r)(n + 2^r))$. Choosing $2^r \approx n$ balances the two terms and gives $\Theta(\beta n/\log n)$. For a million 32-bit keys that is $r = 16$ (two passes); in practice 8-bit digits are common because the 256-entry count array is cache friendly (@sec-lts-a3-base).
:::

**7. How does radix sort handle negative integers?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Either add $-\min$ to every key and subtract it afterwards, or (for fixed-width integers) flip the sign bit, which maps the signed range onto the unsigned range in the same order; sort as unsigned, then flip back. Plain digit extraction on negatives gives the wrong order (@sec-lts-a3-neg).
:::

**8. LSD or MSD radix sort for strings?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
LSD for fixed-length strings (IDs, codes, equal-length keys): simple, stable, $\Theta(w(n + R))$. MSD for variable-length strings: it recurses into groups sharing a prefix, needs an "ended" bucket below every character, and reads only the distinguishing prefixes; it needs a cutoff to insertion sort because each call pays for an $R$-entry count array (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
:::

**9. Give the expected-time argument for bucket sort and an input that defeats it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $n$ uniform keys in $n$ buckets, each bucket size $n_i$ is binomial with $p = 1/n$, so $\mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$. Insertion sort on bucket $i$ costs $O(n_i^2)$, so the expected total is $\Theta(n) + n \cdot O(1) = \Theta(n)$. If all keys fall into one bucket (say all in $[0, 1/n)$), the insertion sort there costs $\Theta(n^2)$ (@sec-lts-a4-proof).
:::

**10. Find all missing numbers in an array with $1 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le n$, in $O(1)$ extra space.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sign marking: for each value $x$, negate slot `abs(x) - 1` if it is positive; afterwards every still-positive slot $i$ means value $i + 1$ never appeared. $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space. Use `abs` because a slot may already have been negated when you read it (@sec-lts-a5, @sec-lts-p2-a).
:::

**11. "First missing positive" in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The answer is in $[1, n+1]$, so only values in $[1, n]$ matter. Cyclic placement: while `a[i]` is in range and its home slot does not already hold it, swap it home. Then the first $i$ with `a[i] != i + 1` gives $i + 1$, else $n + 1$. At most $n$ swaps in total (@sec-lts-p2-b).
:::

**12. Top $k$ frequent elements in linear time?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Count with a hash map, then bucket the values by frequency (`buckets[f]`, $f \in [1, n]$) and scan from $f = n$ down, stopping after $k$ values. $O(n)$ time and space. A size-$k$ heap gives $O(n + A\log k)$, quickselect expected $O(n + A)$ (@sec-lts-p3-b).
:::

**13. "Two indices within $k$ whose values are within $t$": a linear-time solution?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Buckets of width $t + 1$ keyed by $\lfloor x/(t+1) \rfloor$, holding only the last $k$ elements. A value already in the same bucket is a match; a value in a neighbouring bucket is a match if within $t$; otherwise insert and evict the element that left the window. $O(n)$ expected time, $O(k)$ space. Use a real floor for negative values (@sec-lts-p5-b).
:::

**14. For each, choose counting, radix, bucket or comparison sort: (a) $10^7$ ages in $[0, 120]$; (b) $10^6$ floats uniform in $[0, 1)$; (c) $10^6$ arbitrary 64-bit integers; (d) dates as (year, month, day).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) Counting sort: $k = 121$, $O(n)$. (b) Bucket sort: expected $O(n)$. (c) Either a comparison sort or LSD radix with 8- or 16-bit digits; radix is linear but with 4 to 8 passes over the data, and a good library sort is often competitive, so measure. (d) LSD radix: stable counting sort by day ($k = 31$), then month ($k = 12$), then year (offset by the earliest year) (@sec-lts-a3, @sec-lts-a4, @sec-lts-a6).
:::

**15. Is counting sort in place? Can it be made in place?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The stable version is not: it writes into a separate output array of size $n$, plus the $k$-cell count array. An in-place version exists (the "American flag sort" style of cycling each element to its bucket's next free slot), but it is not stable, so it cannot serve as the inner sort of LSD radix. When the keys are bare numbers, the histogram form can overwrite the input in place from the counts, using only the $O(k)$ count array (@sec-lts-a1, @sec-lts-a2).
:::

**16. Why do standard libraries use comparison sorts if radix sort is linear?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A library sort must work for any type with a comparator, where radix sort does not apply. Radix sort also needs $O(n + b)$ extra memory, several passes over the data, and per-type digit extraction (signs, floats, strings), and its advantage appears mainly for large arrays of short fixed-width keys. A comparison sort like introsort or Timsort is general, in place or nearly so, and adaptive to presorted input (@sec-lts-a6).
:::

## Summary

<!-- The callout-important below is copied into the Cheat Sheets appendix: make it stand alone. -->

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Counting sort** keys in $[0, k)$: count, prefix sums ($C[v]$ = #keys $\le v$), place scanning backward with `B[--C[key]] = x`. $\Theta(n + k)$ time and space, stable (@sec-lts-a2).
- **LSD radix sort** one stable counting sort per digit, least significant first; $\Theta(d(n + b))$; for $\beta$-bit keys pick $r$-bit digits with $2^r \approx n$ (@sec-lts-a3).
- **Signed keys** offset by the minimum, or flip the sign bit, before radix sorting (@sec-lts-a3-neg).
- **MSD radix sort** for variable-length strings: counting sort on character $d$ with an "ended" bucket first, recurse into each group (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
- **Bucket sort** $n$ buckets over a known interval, insertion sort each, concatenate; expected $\Theta(n)$ for uniform keys because $\mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$ (@sec-lts-a4).
- **Value-as-index** values in $[1, n]$: sign marking or cyclic placement, $O(1)$ extra space; guard the range (@sec-lts-a5).
- **Frequency as bucket** `buckets[count].append(item)`, scan from $n$ down (@sec-lts-p3).
- **Pigeonhole buckets** width $t + 1$: same bucket means within $t$; within $t$ means same or neighbouring bucket (@sec-lts-p5-b).
- **Decision** verify the key promise in the constraints; if there is none, use a comparison sort (@sec-lts-a6).
:::

- The $\Omega(n\log n)$ bound binds only comparison sorts; using a key as an address escapes it, at the price of memory proportional to the key range (A1).
- Stable counting sort is the workhorse: count, prefix sums, place. The direction of the placement scan must match the kind of positions (end or start) or stability is lost (A2).
- LSD radix sort is $d$ stable counting sorts, least significant first; the induction proof uses stability in the tie case and the pass order to let the newest digit dominate (A3).
- The digit size is a tuning knob: $\Theta((\beta/r)(n + 2^r))$, balanced near $2^r \approx n$.
- MSD radix sort handles strings of any length by recursing inside groups; LSD needs fixed-width keys (A3).
- Bucket sort's linearity is an *expected* bound over uniform inputs, proved with $\mathbb{E}[n_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$; skewed inputs break it (A4).
- With values in $[1, n]$ the input array can be its own histogram (A5, P2, P5).
- Counts, embedded positions and digits are all small integers, so they can all be indices: frequency buckets (P3), direct placement (P4), radix passes (P6).
- Read the constraints first: they decide between counting, radix, bucket and comparison sorts (A6).

- [Sedgewick & Wayne, *Algorithms* 4th ed., §5.1 String Sorts](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/) — key-indexed counting, LSD and MSD string sorts and three-way string quicksort, with code and the cutoff discussion (@sec-lts-a3-msd).
- [MIT 6.006 (Spring 2020), Lecture 5: Linear Sorting](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/resources/lecture-5-linear-sorting/) — direct-access sorts, tuple sorts, counting sort and radix sort from first principles, with lecture notes and video.
- [Wikipedia — Counting sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_sort) — the prefix-sum formulation and its variants (@sec-lts-a2).
- [Wikipedia — Radix sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radix_sort) — LSD and MSD, in-place variants, history (@sec-lts-a3).
- [Wikipedia — Bucket sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucket_sort) — the average-case analysis with $k$ buckets and the worst case (@sec-lts-a4).
- [Competitive Programmer's Handbook (Laaksonen)](https://cses.fi/book/book.pdf) — chapter 3: sorting theory, the lower bound and counting sort, from the contest point of view.
